name: Göbekli Tepe
info: Göbekli Tepe is a Neolithic site in Upper Mesopotamia, in modern Turkey, inhabited from around 9500 BCE to at least 8000 BCE and known for circular enclosures of T-shaped stone pillars, among the oldest known megaliths.

facts.made: Pre-Pottery Neolithic people of Upper Mesopotamia, described as hunter-gatherers who supplemented their diet with early forms of domesticated cereal; excavated from 1995 by Klaus Schmidt
facts.form: A tell 15 m high and 8 ha in extent on a limestone plateau, with circular enclosures of 10 to 30 m in diameter whose walls hold T-shaped limestone pillars, later rectangular rooms, domestic buildings, quarries and rock-cut cisterns
facts.where: Near the village of Örencik in Şanliurfa Province, Turkey, in the Taş Tepeler, in the foothills of the Taurus Mountains above the Harran plain
facts.known: T-shaped pillars among the oldest known megaliths; carved reliefs of foxes, boars, snakes and vultures; the Lion Pillar Building; a rainwater harvesting system; the debate over settling down and farming; UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2018

t: The earliest exposed structures were built between 9500 and 9000 BCE and the site stayed in use until around 8000 BCE, so it belongs to the first phase of permanent settlement anywhere in the world.

Its purpose is not settled: Klaus Schmidt saw a ritual centre visited by nomadic bands, while findings published in 2019 point to a settlement with domestic buildings, cereal processing and a water supply.
Landslides damaged the enclosures during the occupation, and the site was later left, partly farmed, and misread as a graveyard before Schmidt began excavating it in 1995.
dyk: Before archaeologists documented it, local people knew the hill in Kurdish as Girê Mirazan, 'Wish Hill', and considered it a sacred place; the Turkish name Göbekli Tepe means 'Potbelly Hill'.
ev: The earliest exposed structures were built, towards the end of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A
The site was significantly expanded, with new walls that incorporated the first monolithic T-shaped pillars
A second major landslide probably led to the abandonment of enclosure D
The site went out of use, or perhaps slightly later, and smaller groups later lived among the ruins
A survey directed by Halet Çambel and Robert John Braidwood first noted the site
Klaus Schmidt began excavations and soon unearthed the first of the T-shaped pillars
UNESCO designated Göbekli Tepe a World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
Göbekli Tepe was built and occupied during the earliest part of the Southwest Asian Neolithic, the Pre-Pottery Neolithic (c. 9600–7000 BCE). It began at the end of the last Ice Age and produced the earliest evidence for permanent human settlements in the world. One of the earliest known sites, Körtik Tepe, dated to 10,700–9250 BCE, may have been a predecessor of the artistic and material culture of Upper Mesopotamia that includes Göbekli Tepe and the other Taş Tepeler sites. Archaeologists have long associated these settlements with the Neolithic Revolution, the transition from hunting and gathering to agriculture, but disagree on whether farming caused people to settle down or settling down caused people to adopt farming.

The site lies near the village of Örencik in Şanliurfa Province, on a flat limestone plateau in the foothills of the Taurus Mountains. The climate was wetter than today, and an open steppe with wild cereals, including einkorn, wheat and barley, and herds of wild sheep, wild goat, gazelle and equids surrounded the hill. The hilltop gave the builders soft limestone bedrock and the flint to work it. T-shaped pillars like those of Göbekli Tepe are unique to the Urfa region but occur at most Pre-Pottery Neolithic sites there, including Nevalı Çori and Karahan Tepe.
sections.content:
The first circular enclosures range from 10 to 30 m in diameter, with T-shaped limestone pillars set evenly within thick interior walls of unworked stone. Four have been unearthed, and geophysical surveys indicate 16 more, each enclosing up to eight pillars, amounting to nearly 200 in all. Two taller pillars face one another at the centre of each circle, and stone benches for sitting stand inside. Whether the circles were roofed is uncertain. Later enclosures were rectangular, with polished lime floors, and a pair of pillars carved with lions gave the Lion Pillar Building its name.

Many pillars are carved, typically in low relief and sometimes in high relief. Most carvings show animals, mostly serpents, foxes and boars, but also gazelle, mouflon, onager, ducks and vultures; insofar as they can be identified, the animals are male and often aggressive. Abstract H-shaped symbols, crescents and disks also appear. The T-shape is itself anthropomorphic, with the shaft as the body and the top as the head, and some pillars have carved arms, hands and loincloths. The central pillars of enclosure D represent humans with arms, a belt and a cloth. A reassembled 'totem pole' of the early Pre-Pottery Neolithic B is 192 centimetres tall and shows three figures with snakes carved on either side.
sections.making:
Radiocarbon dating shows that the earliest exposed structures were built between 9500 and 9000 BCE and that the site was significantly expanded in the early 9th millennium BCE. It remained in use until around 8000 BCE, or perhaps slightly later. The revised chronology has eight phases spanning at least 1,500 years. The pillar slabs were transported from bedrock pits about 100 m from the hilltop, where workers used flint points to cut through the limestone. Domestic buildings were round-oval at first and increasingly rectangular over time.

Archaeologists disagree on how much labour was needed. Klaus Schmidt, using Thor Heyerdahl's experiments with the moai of Rapa Nui as a reference, estimated that moving the pillars alone must have involved hundreds of people. His team interpreted the site as built by a large, non-resident workforce, coerced or enticed there by a small religious elite. Others estimate that just 7–14 people could have moved the pillars using ropes and water or another lubricant. Experiments at the site itself suggested that all the exposed Pre-Pottery Neolithic B structures could have been built by 12–24 people in less than four months, a number thought to be within the capability of a single extended family or village community.
sections.reception:
Schmidt, who led the excavation from 1995, thought Göbekli Tepe was a ritual centre to which small nomadic hunter-gatherer bands from across the region came for periodic building projects and great feasts before scattering again. Butchered bones of deer, gazelle, pigs and geese were identified as refuse from food prepared for the congregants, and gazelle were only seasonally present, which suggests that feasts were timed to the peak of game. Schmidt presumed shamanic practices and suggested that the pillars represent human forms, perhaps ancestors. He and the zooarchaeologist Joris Peters argued that, since many of the animals are predators, the stones may have been meant to stave off evils through magic or served as totems. Gheorghiu reads the iconography as a cosmogonic map relating the community to the landscape and the cosmos.

Since Schmidt's death in 2014 the assumption that the site was strictly cultic and uninhabited has been challenged, including by the suggestion that the structures were large communal houses. Findings published in 2019 suggest a settlement with domestic structures, extensive cereal processing and a water supply. According to Rémi Hadad, the view of a regional ceremonial centre is giving way to one in which ritual and profane functions coexist. No definitive purpose has been determined, and claims that the site was an astronomical observatory have been largely rejected by the team working there.
sections.survival:
The enclosures lay over 10 metres below the highest areas and suffered several landslides while the site was occupied. A severe one at the end of the early Pre-Pottery Neolithic B inundated enclosure D with rubble, sediments, burials and midden deposits, and led to repairs and stabilisation, including terrace walls. A second major landslide probably led to the enclosure's abandonment around the late 9th millennium BCE. It is unknown why existing pillars were buried every few decades and replaced by new stones in a smaller concentric ring inside the older one. Smaller groups returned to live among the ruins after the Neolithic structures were abandoned.

Known locally in Kurdish as Girê Mirazan or Xerabreşkê, the hill was considered a sacred place before archaeologists documented it. A 1963 survey directed by Halet Çambel and Robert John Braidwood first noted the site, and Peter Benedict mistook the tops of the T-shaped pillars for grave markers. Farmers had moved rocks into clearance piles and apparently tried to break up some pillars, mistaking them for ordinary large rocks. In October 1994 Schmidt, guided by Mahmut Yıldız, whose family owned the land, re-examined the place and began excavations the following year.
sections.legacy:
Göbekli Tepe has played a prominent role in the debate over whether farming caused settlement or the reverse, as a monumental complex on a rocky mountaintop with no clear evidence of agricultural cultivation. Its pillars are among the world's oldest known megaliths, and the structures have been popularly described as the 'world's first temple[s]'. Its architecture and iconography are similar to those of other contemporary sites nearby, such as Karahan Tepe.

After Schmidt died in 2014, work continued as a joint project of Istanbul University, the Şanlıurfa Museum and the German Archaeological Institute, under the direction of Necmi Karul, with recent excavations limited and focused on documentation and conservation. UNESCO designated the site a World Heritage Site in 2018, recognising 'one of the first manifestations of human-made monumental architecture'. Around a tenth of it has been excavated. In 2018 Çiğdem Köksal Schmidt, an archaeologist and the widow of Klaus Schmidt, said that concrete and heavy equipment used to build a walkway had damaged the site; the Ministry of Culture and Tourism responded that no concrete was used and no damage had occurred.

summary: Göbekli Tepe, in the Taş Tepeler of modern Turkey, was inhabited from around 9500 BCE to at least 8000 BCE. Its circular enclosures of T-shaped, carved pillars are among the oldest known megaliths, and whether it was a ritual centre or a settlement is still debated.
references: Steven Mithen, After the Ice: A global human history, 20,000–5000 BC (Harvard University Press, 2004)
Klaus Schmidt, Sie bauten die ersten Tempel. Das rätselhafte Heiligtum der Steinzeitjäger (C.H. Beck, 2006)
Klaus Schmidt, Le premier temple: Göbekli Tepe (CNRS éditions, 2015)

It also says 'Radiocarbon dating places the construction of these early circles c. 9000 BCE' in the architecture section, which differs slightly; the text uses the chronology section.
Abandonment of enclosure D: the article says 'late 9th millennium BCE' (phase 6 and landslides sections); phases 6-7 are 'late 9th to early 8th millennium BCE'.
The article gives the 1994/1995 sequence and 'only three tombs' by Schmidt, but also 2017 skull fragments; the burials and skull cult were left out for space.
Left out: phallic figures, the Sumerian Ekur myth, the Roman watchtower and quarry, tool counts, enclosure triangle (Haklay and Gopher).
Hadad's quotation and the 'world's first temple' phrase are quoted as the article has them.
